core.text: When a sentence reports an order, a request or a wish, the thing wanted goes into a clause with **ut / ne + subjunctive (the form for what someone asks or orders someone to do)**: *imperat ut mercēdem solvat* — he orders him to pay the rent; *ōrat nē sē verberet* — he begs him not to beat him. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus substantīvus: ut, nē*.
English uses *to*: *he told the farmer to pay*, *she asked her not to leave*. The *to*-phrase is the command.
Verb of ordering, asking, warning or wishing + ut (nē for 'not') + subjunctive. Lead-ins: imperō, rogō, ōrō, moneō, postulō, cūrō, hortor, volō.

invented.la: Māter fīliō imperat nē in viā lūdat.
invented.en: The mother orders her son not to play in the street.

core.text: After a verb of doing the same *ut* + subjunctive is **ut / ne + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)** — it says why. After *imperat, rogat, monet* it says what was ordered. Ask: is *ut* completing a verb of telling, or explaining an action?

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) call this the substantive subjunctive: a noun clause for a wish, command or tendency rather than a fact. Their examples: *dux imperat ut mīlitēs sequantur*; *volō ut omnēs veniāmus*; *mōs est Rōmānīs ut ad cēnam discumbant*; and *accidit ut …* / *fit ut …* (it happens that …).

The clause verb is present subjunctive after a present main verb and imperfect after a past one (*rogāvit ut nārrāret*); that pairing is the sequence of tenses. Two verbs of ordering skip *ut*: *iubeō* and *vetō* take the accusative + infinitive (*iubet eum venīre*). Verbs of saying and thinking never take *ut*; they take the accusative + infinitive (*dīcit eum venīre*). A second negative in the clause is *nēve*: *cūrā nē ovēs aberrent* — and *nēve silvam petant*.

teach.title: Reporting an order
teach.say: When a sentence tells you what somebody was told to do, the order itself becomes a clause: **ut / nē + subjunctive (the form for what someone asks or orders someone to do)**. *Dominus servō imperat ut labōret* — the master orders the slave to work. English uses a plain 'to'; Latin uses *ut* and puts the verb into the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). The *ut* clause is the words that were said.

check.ask: Tap the word that carries the order.

teach.title: ut and a subjunctive, never an infinitive
teach.say: The clause opens with **ut** and its verb is always subjunctive. Latin does not say *monet tacēre*; it says *monet ut taceat*. When you read it, translate *ut* as nothing at all — 'warns him to keep quiet' — and turn the subjunctive into the plain English 'to' form. When you write it, the English 'to' is your signal to put in *ut* and change the verb.

teach.title: nē for what must not happen
teach.say: A negative order swaps **nē** in for *ut*: *monet nē currant*, 'warns them not to run'. Nothing else moves — same lead-in verb, same subjunctive, same word order. If you ever find yourself writing *ut nōn* after a verb of ordering or asking, it should have been *nē*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of verberō that nē needs here.

teach.title: Which verbs set it off
teach.say: These clauses hang on one family of verbs: *imperō* (order), *ōrō* (beg), *moneō* (warn), *cūrō* (see to it), *postulō* (demand), *volō* (want). One common verb refuses the pattern: *iubeō* (order) takes a plain infinitive instead — *Dāvum venīre iubet*, 'he orders Davus to come'. Meet *ut* or *nē* after any of the first family and the clause is the order itself.

teach.title: Not a purpose clause
teach.say: *ut* + subjunctive also says why something is done — **ut / nē + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)**. What tells them apart is the verb in front. After a verb of telling (*imperat, ōrat, monet*) the *ut* clause is what was said; after any other verb it is the reason for doing it. Ask: is this clause completing a verb of telling, or explaining an action?

check.ask: What is bibat here — the order itself, or the doctor's reason?
